newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poll-Germans oppose both euro, anti-Euro campaign. [CORRECTED 11:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Poll-Germans oppose both euro, anti-Euro campaign. [CORRECTED 11:51 GMT]

text.p: Most German voters want the European Union's planned single currency to be delayed but a majority do not want the euro to be a campaign issue in next year's general election, a new opinion poll released on Monday showed.

An Emnid poll for the news magazine Der Spiegel said 56 percent of those surveyed did not want the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to make the euro a campaign issue while 42 percent thought it should be debated before the October vote.

But, if the SPD did decide to use the issue, 81 (corrects by inserting dropped number) percent of those surveyed said it should argue for a delay in the 1999 target date for its introduction. Only 18 percent said the SPD should support the planned launching of the euro as it now stands.

The apparently contradictory result of the poll reflected a split in German public opinion between strong concern over the stability which a single currency could achieve and a broad general support for European integration.

Echoing that pro-European overview, President Roman Herzog -- who is supposed to be above politics -- recently urged the party not to make the EU's economic and monetary union (EMU) an issue for the election campaign.

A leading analyst from another German pollster, Electoral Research Group, said he thoughta decision by Christian Democratic Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who turned 67 last week, to run for re-election had effectively neutralised EMU as a campaign issue.
"Now most (voters) will be satisfied that Kohl is managing this," Dieter Roth said.
The Emnid survey was taken on April 2 and 3 with a sample of 1,000 people
